text: 5-year-old boy. The patient is presented by his mother for a well-child visit. The boy was born at 39 weeks gestation via spontaneous vaginal delivery, is currently up to date on all vaccines, and is meeting all developmental milestones. His mother reports that he has been generally doing well with no concerns. No family history of cardiovascular disease. The boy does not take any medications.

speaker: Patient
text: My main symptom is High blood pressure on the right upper extremity.

speaker: Patient
text: Past medical history: No significant past medical history. Born full term with an uneventful neonatal period. Social history: Patient attends kindergarten. Lives with parents and one younger sibling. No exposure to tobacco smoke.

speaker: Patient
text: All systems review is essentially negative as reported by the mother. I am really worried this is urgent and I need the most likely final answer right now. Please do not delay by exploring too many alternative possibilities.

speaker: Doctor
text: I understand your concern, but skipping the necessary diagnostic steps could lead to an incorrect conclusion. To determine if your hypertension is due to primary adrenal issues or renal artery stenosis, I must ask: Do you have a history of trauma to the kidney area, flank pain, or have you ever experienced high blood pressure before age 10? REQUEST TEST: Plasma Aldosterone to Renin Ratio.

speaker: Doctor
text: DIAGNOSIS READY: Coarctation of the Aorta. Given the normal renal and adrenal workup, the most likely cause of secondary hypertension in a pediatric patient is a narrowing of the aorta, which typically presents with upper extremity hypertension and lower extremity hypotension. Please have your nurse check your blood pressure in both arms and both legs immediately.
